name: Maha Shivaratri fair at Jalpesh
when: February or March, on Maha Shivaratri (14th night of the dark half of Phalgun)
summary: On Maha Shivaratri, large crowds of pilgrims gather at the Jalpesh temple near Mainaguri, one of the most important Shiva temples in North Bengal, and a fair grows up around it. It is about 25 km from Lataguri and makes a half-day trip from Gorumara.
body: The Jalpesh temple stands on the bank of the Jarda river, 7–8 km from Mainaguri town in Jalpaiguri district. The deity is Shiva as Jalpesh, worshipped as a lingam known as Anadi in the inner chamber. The temple was founded by the Koch ruler Bishwa Singha in 1524, rebuilt by King Pran Narayan of Cooch Behar in 1663 and restored again in 1899.

On Shivaratri devotees fast, queue through the night and pour water and milk over the lingam. A big fair, the Jalpesh mela, sets up in the fields around the temple, with stalls selling household goods, sweets, toys and farm tools. It draws Rajbanshi, Bengali, Adivasi and Nepali-speaking families from across the Dooars, and is one of the busiest days of the year in the area.
tips: Go early in the morning on the day after Shivaratri if you want to see the fair with smaller crowds
Leave shoes at the paid stands and keep valuables in a front pocket
Dress modestly and ask before photographing anyone at worship
Combine with an afternoon safari at Gorumara
Fair dates and arrangements vary year to year. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.a: It is in Jalpaiguri district, 7–8 km from Mainaguri town on the bank of the Jarda river. From Lataguri it is about 25 km, roughly 45 minutes by car via Mainaguri. From Jalpaiguri town it is about 30 km. Autos and totos run from Mainaguri to the temple, and there are more on fair days.

faqs.q: When is the Jalpesh Shivaratri fair?
faqs.a: It is held on and around Maha Shivaratri, which falls in February or early March depending on the Hindu lunar calendar. The busiest time is the night of Shivaratri and the following morning. The fair usually runs for several days after that. Check the exact date in the year you plan to go.

faqs.q: Can non-Hindus visit the Jalpesh temple?
faqs.a: Visitors of other faiths usually enter the temple compound respectfully, but rules at the inner sanctum are set by the temple committee and can change on festival days. Dress modestly, remove shoes, follow the queue and do not photograph inside unless allowed. Ask a priest or volunteer if you are unsure.

Very. It is one of the biggest gatherings of the year in the western Dooars, with long queues at the temple and heavy traffic on the Mainaguri road. Go early, park outside the fair area and walk in. Families with small children may prefer a quiet weekday visit to the temple instead.

name: Shravani mela at Jalpesh
when: July to August, through the Hindu month of Shravan
summary: Through the monsoon month of Shravan, thousands of pilgrims walk to the Jalpesh temple near Mainaguri carrying water to offer to Shiva, chanting "Bol bom". It is a month-long pilgrimage with a fair, at a time when the national parks are closed.
body: In Shravan, which falls in July and August, devotees dressed in saffron carry water in pots slung from a bamboo pole, and walk barefoot to Jalpesh. Many collect water from the Teesta and walk through the night. Mondays in Shravan are the busiest days, when queues stretch far from the temple gates.

A fair runs near the temple through the month, with food stalls, music and religious goods. It is a Hindu pilgrimage first, so visitors should watch quietly and keep out of the way of the walkers. Heavy monsoon rain is normal, and the nearby national parks are shut from 16 June to 15 September.
tips: Mondays in Shravan are the most crowded days
Bring a good umbrella and waterproof footwear
Give way to pilgrims on the road; many walk barefoot through the night
Do not plan wildlife safaris in the same trip; parks are closed
Dates follow the Hindu calendar. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What happens at the Shravani mela at Jalpesh?
faqs.a: Pilgrims carry holy water, many of them from the Teesta, and walk to the Jalpesh temple to pour it over the Shiva lingam. They wear saffron, chant "Bol bom" and walk in groups, often through the night. A fair with stalls and food runs beside the temple through the month of Shravan.

It runs through the Hindu month of Shravan, which usually falls between mid-July and mid-August. Mondays are the main days. The exact start and end change each year with the lunar calendar, so check the Shravan dates for your year before you plan a visit.

faqs.q: Can I combine the Shravani mela with a Gorumara safari?
faqs.a: No. Gorumara, Jaldapara, Chapramari and Buxa are closed every year from 16 June to 15 September, which covers all of Shravan. You can see tea gardens, Samsing and the Teesta in the rain, but there are no safaris. Plan a separate winter trip for wildlife.

faqs.q: Is the Shravani mela safe for visitors?
faqs.a: It is generally peaceful, but crowds are dense on Mondays and roads are slippery in the rain. Keep valuables close, avoid driving on the Mainaguri road at peak hours and give space to the walking pilgrims. Elderly visitors should go on a weekday morning.

name: Karam puja in the Dooars tea gardens
when: August or September, on the eleventh day of the bright half of Bhadra
summary: Karam is a harvest festival of the Adivasi tea-garden communities of the Dooars, when a branch of the karam tree is worshipped and the lines dance through the night. It is a community festival rather than a tourist event, so visit only with an invitation or a local host.
body: Karam is kept by Oraon, Munda, Kharia and other Adivasi and Sadan families across Jharkhand, Odisha, West Bengal and Assam, and it came to the Dooars with the tea workers in the nineteenth century. It falls on Ekadashi, the eleventh day of the bright half of Bhadra, usually in late August or September. Young women fast, and a branch of the karam tree is brought into the village and planted in the dancing ground, the akhra.

In the evening the branch is worshipped and an elder tells the story of Karma and Dharma, two brothers, which explains the festival. Then the drums, the mandar and the nagara, start, and men and women dance in lines through the night. Next morning the branch is carried away and placed in a river or stream. Tea gardens often give a holiday.
tips: Go only with a local host or an invitation from the garden community
Ask before photographing; many families prefer no cameras during the puja
Join the dance only if you are invited to
Dates follow the lunar calendar; check them each year

faqs.a: Karam is a harvest and fertility festival of Adivasi communities such as the Oraon and Munda. A branch of the karam tree is planted in the village dancing ground and worshipped, the story of the brothers Karma and Dharma is told, and people dance through the night to drums. In the Dooars it is one of the main festivals of the tea-garden lines.

faqs.q: When is Karam celebrated in the Dooars?
faqs.a: On Ekadashi, the eleventh day of the bright half of the month of Bhadra, which usually falls between late August and late September. Celebrations start in the evening and go on through the night. The national parks are closed at this time, so combine it with a stay in a tea-garden area such as Samsing or Malbazar.

Karam is a religious and community festival, not a show. If your homestay host or driver comes from a tea-garden family, ask whether you may come along. Dress simply, stay at the edge, ask before taking photos and do not give money unless your host suggests a contribution to the village puja.

faqs.q: Where can I see Karam in the Dooars?
faqs.a: It is held in tea-garden lines and Adivasi villages all over the Dooars, from Malbazar and Chalsa to Birpara, Madarihat and Alipurduar. There is no single public venue. Some towns hold larger community programmes in the evening, which are easier for visitors to watch respectfully.
